summary: Defines MIB objects for managing DS1, J1, E1, DS2 and E2 interfaces, which are telephone-company digital line types. It is a companion to the managed-object documents for DS0, DS3/E3 and related interfaces.

eli5.summary: Phone companies use digital lines called T1 and E1. This note lists the gauges that let a manager check how those lines are doing.

questions: snmp objects for t1 and e1 interfaces
snmp objects for t1 and e1
subtitle: The SNMP objects for monitoring T1, E1, J1, DS2 and E2 digital telephone lines.

tldr.problem: Devices with DS1, J1, E1, DS2 or E2 interfaces needed one common, standard way to be configured and monitored by SNMP managers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the DS1-MIB module: configuration, current, interval and total tables, plus line status, loopback and performance counters. It builds on the standard interfaces table and adopts ANSI T1.231 style terminology for errors and alarms.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3895, adding J1 line types, a line impedance object and deprecating the degraded-minute objects.

today: RFC 4805 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3895. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Scope and Line Types
sections.content:
RFC 4805 defines a MIB (Management Information Base) module for interfaces where the medium is DS1, J1, E1, DS2 or E2. It applies to the interface type ds1 (18) and is a companion to the documents for DS0, DS3/E3 and SONET/SDH interfaces.

The definitions rest on the AT&T T-1 Superframe (D4) and Extended Superframe (ESF) formats, and on the CCITT G.703 and ITU-T G.704 recommendations, referred to as E1. J1 follows Japanese JT-G704, JT-G706 and JT-I431. The line disciplines are judged similar enough that separate MIBs are unwarranted, so the older e1(19) and g703at2mb(67) interface types were obsoleted and there is no special type for J1.

The RFC aligns the MIB closely with what can generally be read from deployed devices. J2 interfaces are not supported.
sections.eli5: There are several cousins of the same kind of phone line. Instead of one rulebook for each cousin, there is a single rulebook that covers them all.

sections.title: Interface Table Usage and Stacking
sections.content:
For the DS1 layer only the ifGeneralInformationGroup of the interfaces MIB needs to be supported. The RFC gives per-object guidance: ifType is ds1(18), ifSpeed is the line rate, and ifPhysAddress carries the Circuit Identifier, or a zero-length octet string if none is assigned.

The object dsx1IfIndex is deprecated. Instead the ifStackTable shows which interfaces are attached to which, for example a router with a shelf of CSUs, or DS1 interfaces stacked on a DS2 or E2 interface. The RFC stresses this is not meant to represent TDM connections in general.

Channelization is explained with examples. A DS3 channelized into DS1s gives 28 DS1 entries, and each DS1 channelized into DS0s gives 24 DS0s. A DS3 channelized into DS2s gives 7 DS2s, each holding 4 DS1s. The mappings are recorded in the dsx1ChanMappingTable.
sections.eli5: Every line gets a numbered slot in a big list. A second list says which slots are plugged into which, like noting that these four small pipes all feed into one big pipe.

sections.title: Loopbacks
sections.content:
A loopback sends a line's signal back where it came from, for testing. dsx1LoopbackConfig is the desired state, and a manager can request line loopback, payload loopback (ESF framing only), inward loopback, dual loopback (line plus inward) or no loopback. The actual state is reported in the bitmap dsx1LoopbackStatus, which also records the source of each loopback.

The far end can request loopbacks too, through the Facility Data Link (FDL) channel with ESF or inband with D4, but only line loopback, payload loopback (ESF) and no loopback.

The rules: the far end cannot undo loopbacks set by a manager, while a manager can undo those set by the far end. A line loopback and an inward loopback can coexist, and only those two. If a manager has set an inward loopback and the far end later requests and then clears a line loopback, the inward loopback stays in place.
sections.eli5: A loopback is like shouting into a canyon and listening for your own echo to check that the line works. The person who set up the test is the one who gets to end it.

sections.title: Error Counts and Performance Intervals
sections.content:
Performance parameters are accumulated in 15-minute intervals. An agent keeps up to 96 intervals (24 hours), plus a rolling 24-hour total. Counting continues while the interface is down. The counters use Gauge32-based textual conventions because values can decrease when Unavailable Seconds straddle an interval boundary.

The main counters are seconds-based: Line Errored Seconds (one or more line coding violations), Errored Seconds, Severely Errored Seconds (SES), Severely Errored Framing Seconds, Controlled Slip Seconds and, for ESF only, Bursty Errored Seconds (more than 1 and fewer than 320 path coding violations). For ESF, an SES has 320 or more path coding violations, an out-of-frame defect or an AIS defect; for E1-CRC the threshold is 832.

An interface becomes unavailable from the onset of 10 contiguous SESs and available again after 10 contiguous seconds without SES. While unavailable, only the Unavailable Seconds count increases. Because this can only be known after 10 seconds, an agent either adjusts counts retroactively or delays statistics by 10 seconds, as sketched in Appendix B. A linkDown trap is sent only once the unavailable state is certain, but carries the time of the first unavailable second.
sections.eli5: Every second the line is graded like a school day: fine, a few mistakes, or a disaster. Ten disaster days in a row and the line is marked closed until it has ten good seconds in a row.

sections.title: Defects, Alarms and Line Status
sections.content:
The RFC defines error events (such as bipolar violations and excessive zeroes), defects (such as Out of Frame and Alarm Indication Signal) and failure states. Failures are reported in the bitmap object dsx1LineStatus, where several bits can be set at once and dsx1NoAlarm is set if and only if no other flag is set.

Examples of failures: the Far End Alarm (called Yellow Alarm for DS1 and J1, Distant Alarm for E1, Remote Alarm for DS2); Loss of Frame (red alarm); Loss of Signal; AIS; and, for E1 only, TS16 AIS and Loss of Multiframe. For DS1, Loss of Signal is declared upon observing 175 +/- 75 contiguous pulse positions with no pulses. A Loopback Pseudo-Failure is declared when the near end has placed any loopback on the DS1, so one object tells a manager whether the line counts as in service.
sections.eli5: Alarm lights on the dashboard: one for no signal, one for lost track of the beat, one for the other side shouting that something is wrong. The status object holds all the lights at once.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Several read-write objects are sensitive. Setting incorrect values for objects such as dsx1LineType, dsx1LineCoding, dsx1SendCode, dsx1LoopbackConfig and dsx1TransmitClockSource may interrupt traffic. For example, both ends of a DS1/E1 must have the same dsx1LineType for traffic to flow. Setting dsx1CircuitIdentifier wrongly does not harm traffic but can cause a circuit to be misidentified, and enabling dsx1LineStatusChangeTrapEnable can increase trap volume.

Readable objects can also be sensitive, since together they reveal performance and some configuration of the equipment. SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and deploying them is NOT RECOMMENDED. Implementers are RECOMMENDED to use SNMPv3 with its cryptographic authentication and privacy.
sections.eli5: The dials that control the line are powerful. If a stranger turned them, the line could stop working, so only trusted people should be allowed to touch them.

sections.title: Changes From Earlier Versions
sections.content:
This document obsoletes RFC 3895. Compared with it, values were added to dsx1LineType to support J1 types, the object dsx1LineImpedance was added, all degraded-minute (DM) related objects were deprecated following their removal from ITU performance standards, and the compliance statements were updated.

The appendix also traces the history back through RFC 2495 and RFC 1406, which brought SMIv2, ifStackTable examples, DS2 and E2 support, and the loopback status object.
sections.eli5: This is the newest edition of a rulebook. It adds a few new entries, retires some old ones, and keeps the rest.
